sentences.text: Eremopezus eocaenus was a gigantic, presumably flightless bird described as a 'walking hermit' due to its solitary nature. This enormous creature possessed well-developed legs extending from the lower leg to the midfoot and had a body size similar to Mullerornis betsilei.

C. W. Andrews first described the genus in 1904 based on a distal left tibiotarsus, noting that only one species is known from fossil remains. These fossils were found in the Upper Eocene Jebel Qatrani Formation near the Qasr el Sagha escarpment, north of Lake Birket Qarun near Faiyum in Egypt. The rocks containing these fossils were deposited in the Priabonian stage, with the oldest dating to about 36 million years ago and the youngest to no less than 33 million years ago. Fossils were previously thought to be from the Early Oligocene (33-30 Ma), but this is now considered incorrect.

Eremopezus had widely divergent toes capable of flexing through a wide range of positions and strong tendons that provided a firm grip. Researchers suggest Eremopezus behaved similarly to secretarybirds and shoebills in the swamps of the Jebel Qatrani Formation. No known palaeognaths evolved gripping feet like Eremopezus, nor did they thrive in wetland habitats like those in the Jebel Qatrani Formation. Eremopezus likely had white, black, or grey feathers containing eumelanin but little carotenoids and phaeomelinins, typical of higher waterbirds in similar habitats. Piscivory or generalist predation are plausible diets for Eremopezus given its habitat, although many flightless birds are herbivorous or omnivorous. It is hypothesized that E. eocaenus might have been a frugivore or herbivore of swamp forests, though early Neoaves are generally predatory. As a predator, it likely fed mainly on mid-sized terrestrial vertebrates such as large reptiles or small mammals. Unmated birds were probably solitary.

Researchers initially believed Eremopezus was a ratite closely related to the elephant birds of Madagascar. The presence of deep ligamental pits on the distal condyles distinguishes Eremopezus from elephant birds. The tarsometatarsus of Eremopezus resembles that of general ratites like emus or ostriches rather than elephant birds. It is debated whether Eremopezus represents a separate example of ratite bodyplan origins or is a flightless neognath. Eremopezus may belong to a distinct family, Eremopezidae, because its closest relatives are unknown.

Fossils of Eremopezus date to the Late Eocene epoch, though some sources suggest a time range from the Priabonian to the Rupelian, between 37.71 and 27.3 million years ago. Fossils date from a time when the region had more forest and less grassland than it did six million years later, and the habitat likely resembled the modern Niger Delta.

There is a debate regarding whether certain fossil eggshells from the Maghreb belong to Eremopezus or to ostriches. It is debated whether Eremopezus possessed a hook or 'nail' on its bill tip if it was a pelecaniform, and robust conclusions about its habits remain impossible without further fossil data. It is debated whether flightless birds can compete with carnivorous mammals, as the Phorusrhacidae prove that carnivorous flightless birds can thrive alongside mammalian competitors.
